To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the use of high-oleic acid oil in swine diets did not adversely affect storage stability of fresh sausage.

the use of safflower or high oleic sunflower oil to replace a typical corn/ soybean meal diet to growing pigs did not alter the visual properties and stability of low fat pork sausage during 10 weeks storage.

the addition of safflower and sunflower oils to swine diets at levels of up to 10% did not affect the visual properties or storage stability of low fat pork sausage, but the use of canola oil in the diet of growing pigs did affect these characteristics.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new technologies for the production of high-quality meat products with reduced fat and cholesterol content.
the effect of dietary fat on the quality and shelf-life of low-fat pork sausage.
the effects of feeding diets containing high levels of oleate to swine on pork quality and the stability of low-fat pork sausage.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of high oleic safflower or high oleic sunflower oil in the diets of swine did not alter the visual properties or storage stability of fresh sausage.

the addition of 10% safflower or canola oil to the diets of growing-finishing swine did not alter the quality characteristics of fresh pork sausage, but the use of canola oil resulted in less desirable color characteristics.
feeding diets containing high oleic acid oils (sunflower and safflower) to swine does not alter the storage stability of low fat fresh sausage.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

feeding a diet containing a 10% substitution of animal fat, saflower oil or sunflower seed oil did not affect the visual properties of fresh pork sausage, but that canola oil increased the discoloration of the sausage.
the addition of 10% safflower or 10% sunflower oil to a typical corn/ soymeal diet of swine did not affect the visual quality of fresh pork sausage and did not adversely affect its storage stability.

the use of high levels of safflower oil and sunflower oil in the diets of growing-finishing pigs does not adversely affect the storage-stability, sensory properties or consumer acceptance of low-fat pork products.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the visual properties of low-fat sausage are affected by the dietary fat source of the swine.
the use of high-oleic acid oils in the diet of finishing swine does not affect the storage stability of low fat sausage.
the visual properties of low-fat sausage can be improved by feeding a diet containing a high level of oleic acid.
